segments.title: The German command post at the Opéra in 1944
segments.text:
Look towards the Palais Garnier.

Take a moment to study its façade.

The monumental steps. The statues. The columns. The grand perspectives.

This building was designed to impress.

It evokes glittering opera nights, elegant sets, bright lights and fashionable society.

But in August nineteen forty-four, the square in front of you was anything but a gala scene.

German soldiers still occupied positions in the French capital.

Paris was in revolt.

And a German military command post in the Opéra district became one of the flashpoints of those days.

Let's return to the nineteenth of August, nineteen forty-four.

After four years of occupation, events were moving quickly.

Police officers, Resistance fighters and armed groups were trying to regain control of different neighbourhoods.

But German forces were still present.

Paris had not yet been liberated.

Communications were difficult.

And the danger could change from one street to the next.

Photographs taken around the Opéra still show German soldiers, vehicles and military positions.

They're invaluable records.

We don't need to invent a vanished Paris.

We can see uniformed figures standing outside buildings that are still recognisable today.

Compare a window.

The corner of a façade.

The line of an avenue.

The same neighbourhood.

But a very different world.

The following day, the twentieth of August, those tensions lead to a death.

Two French police officers are in the area.

Their names are Michel Guillois and Pierre Gormond.

Guillois is helping deliver an order or message concerning a ceasefire.

The situation is confused.

In insurgent Paris, several efforts to arrange truces or agreements are intended to prevent further fighting.

But none of them makes every German position safe.

Gunfire breaks out near the command post.

According to a family account of the episode, a German officer ordered a sentry on a balcony to fire towards the police officers' vehicle.

That particular detail, about the order and the person who gave it, comes from the family testimony.

We must not present it as an independently established finding.

Michel Guillois is hit.

He dies.

According to the same preserved account, Pierre Gormond is wounded in the leg by two bullets.

This is five days before the Liberation of Paris.

Look up at the windows around you.

For the policemen moving through these streets, the grand architecture offered no special protection.

A German position could still open fire.

An ordinary journey along a familiar road could be fatal.

That's why it would be misleading to tell only the story of the command post's capture on the twenty-fifth of August.

The final assault was preceded by days of fighting, uncertainty and casualties.

The Palais Garnier was drawn into the war well before French armoured vehicles arrived.

Now let's move forward a few days.

On the evening of the twenty-fourth of August, advance elements of the Second French Armoured Division, under General Philippe Leclerc, entered Paris.

On the twenty-fifth, more units moved through the capital.

Resistance fighters, insurgent police and French soldiers began retaking different positions.

But German forces did not vanish all at once.

Each remaining strongpoint could require its own operation.

The Opéra district was one of them.

It's now the twenty-fifth of August.

In the middle of the afternoon, French troops attack the German command post.

Among those taking part is the Eleventh Company of the Third Battalion of the Régiment de marche du Tchad.

It's a rather technical name.

But this regiment was among the formations accompanying the Second Armoured Division on its advance.

The soldiers who arrived here had already endured long campaigns before reaching central Paris.

And an extraordinary historical photograph documents their action.

In the image, you can see a French half-track.

That's a vehicle with wheels at the front and tracks at the back.

It's towing a fifty-seven-millimetre anti-tank gun.

And painted on its side is an extraordinary name.

La Revanche, thirty-nine, forty.

La Revanche, thirty-nine, forty.

The Revenge.

A name painted on a military vehicle, but also a striking reminder of the journey since France's defeat in nineteen forty.

Four years earlier, the French army had collapsed before the German offensive.

Now French soldiers were helping to liberate their capital.

The vehicle's name cannot tell us what every man aboard was thinking.

But it does tell us what the vehicle was called.

And the inscription is visible in the photographic record.

Look again at the avenue as it appears today.

In the picture from nineteen forty-four, dark smoke obscures part of the view.

Ordinary shops and façades stand behind the military vehicles.

Those details matter.

The fighting is taking place in a living neighbourhood.

Not on some isolated battlefield.

A shopfront.

An apartment window.

A carriage entrance.

Completely ordinary features, suddenly caught up in a military operation.

We cannot make people in a photograph speak.

We don't know precisely what each soldier could see beyond the edge of the frame.

But we can identify vehicles, markings, buildings and the documented sequence of events.

That's already a great deal.

And it's how photographs can help us understand history without inventing it.

The French forces advance on the position.

The situation changes.

And then comes the surrender.

In another historical photograph, German servicemen are emerging, with a white flag visible.

French soldiers, Resistance fighters and civilians are gathered around them.

Only a short while earlier, the men holding this position had still been an armed occupying force.

Now they are becoming prisoners.

But let's be precise about what the pictures can establish.

A photograph can show people coming out, uniforms, a white flag and the crowd around them.

It cannot, by itself, reconstruct the entire surrender negotiation or every tactical movement that came before.

The twenty-fifth of August, nineteen forty-four, is remembered as the day Paris was liberated.

That's an accurate description of the wider historical event.

But it can obscure what came before.

The policeman killed on the twentieth.

His wounded colleague.

The last defended positions.

The men still advancing through the streets, unsure what waited around the next corner.

Liberation wasn't a single instant.

It was a succession of fights, orders, surrenders and risks, lived through by different people.

Take a few seconds to look at the Opéra.

Its architecture seems designed to last.

It had survived the fall of the Second Empire, under which construction first began.

It witnessed changes throughout the neighbourhood.

Then the Occupation.

And finally those days of August nineteen forty-four.

There's one last thing to do here.

Look at the historical photograph on your screen and try to place the camera in the real space around you.

Find the line of a cornice.

The position of a statue.

A street corner.

The outline of the Palais Garnier.

You're not watching a reconstruction with actors.

You're looking at an authentic archive, returned to the place where it makes sense.

And suddenly, the distance between nineteen forty-four and today seems a little shorter.

We're now going to travel much further back.

In our imaginations, the opera house will disappear.

So will the wide avenues.

Because our final stop takes place in sixteen fifty-two, when Paris was torn apart by the Fronde.

And when two brothers-in-law decided to settle a quarrel with weapons.
